outputs.L2:
1. The broadcast predicts that by 2050, cultivating land in Massachusetts may resemble farming in present-day Georgia. Everything is changing: no one knows what Georgia will support, where sugar maples will survive, or who will set delicate spiles into cold spring trees to draw their sweet sap. Will syrup come from the northern forest and peaches from Massachusetts?

2. Unmanned attacks and fields of opium poppies. Petroleum slicks and contaminated wells. Regions of drought. Starvation. Battlefields.

3. This small, handcrafted act of intervention—what a gift today offers.

4. The skeptic inside me whispers, why try? This is merely self-absorption. My Yale friend says that wanting to live close to zucchini cannot protect the world from actual hunger. Yet I recall the film about gleaners, where a compassionate priest declares that people who glean because their spirits are hungry deserve nourishment too.

5. Whether in a garden, a field, or the imagination, an ecosystem forms. These cucumbers belong more to art than to science, more to reverie than to planetary action—if those things can truly be divided. Still, as I dig, I encounter something beyond myself: life, vast and nonhuman in its freedom. I tend a piece of earth that anchors me as well—
outputs.L3:
Climate change may transform regional agriculture so profoundly that familiar crops and natural resources shift to entirely new locations. Plants once associated with a particular landscape may no longer thrive there, while changing temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions reshape what can be grown and where. At the same time, environmental destruction, drought, famine, and war expose the severity of the global crises surrounding food, land, and human survival.

Against this immense backdrop, small-scale, artisanal cultivation can appear almost insignificant. A garden cannot end global hunger or repair damaged ecosystems on its own, and the time and care devoted to it may even seem self-indulgent. Yet cultivating a small piece of land can still be understood as a meaningful gift or intervention. Its value lies not only in the food it produces, but also in the attention, responsibility, and hope it embodies.

Gardening may have limited material reach, but it can nourish a different kind of hunger: a spiritual longing for connection, purpose, and participation in the living world. Working the soil brings personal imagination into direct contact with ecological processes. Seeds, insects, weather, decay, and growth all resist complete human control, offering a grounding encounter with nonhuman life. In this way, cultivation becomes both a creative practice and a reminder that human existence is inseparable from the ecosystems that sustain it.
outputs.L4:
Climate change, war, famine, and ecological destruction have made it increasingly difficult to imagine the future of agriculture. Fields are scorched by drought, flooded by violent storms, exhausted by chemicals, or abandoned by people driven from their homes. Food moves through a global system that is both astonishingly productive and profoundly fragile. While some regions produce abundance, others endure hunger; while grain is wasted or diverted, families elsewhere face empty markets and rising prices. Under such conditions, the question of how we will feed ourselves becomes inseparable from questions of politics, justice, and survival.

Against crises of this scale, the act of tending a garden can seem painfully inadequate. A small plot cannot stop a war, cool the atmosphere, restore a vanished forest, or feed millions of displaced people. A few rows of beans and potatoes will not correct the inequalities built into the global food system. Even the most careful gardener must recognize the limits of personal action. It is tempting either to exaggerate the garden’s importance, turning cultivation into a fantasy of self-sufficiency, or to dismiss it entirely as a private comfort without political consequence.

Yet gardening persists. Seeds are pressed into the soil even when the future is uncertain. Beds are weeded, watered, and protected from frost. The gardener works with hope, but not with certainty: rain may fail, insects may arrive, disease may spread, and the harvest may be smaller than expected. Cultivation therefore becomes an education in vulnerability. It teaches that human plans depend upon forces that cannot be commanded and upon forms of life that follow their own purposes.

The garden is never solely a human creation. Worms open passages through the earth; fungi bind roots into hidden networks; bees, moths, and flies carry pollen from flower to flower. Birds take fruit, slugs consume seedlings, and weeds return wherever the soil is disturbed. What appears to be an orderly plot is actually a meeting place of countless lives. The gardener may guide, prune, fence, and select, but control remains partial. Growth belongs to the plants themselves and to the larger world of weather, soil, water, and time.

This recognition does not excuse withdrawal from collective responsibility. Personal cultivation cannot replace political action, humanitarian aid, ecological restoration, or the transformation of destructive agricultural systems. The hunger of strangers cannot be answered merely by enjoying one’s own harvest. If the garden becomes a refuge from reality, it risks shrinking moral concern to the boundaries of private property. Meaningful action must extend beyond the fence: toward solidarity, fair access to land and food, resistance to war, and protection of the living systems on which all agriculture depends.

Still, usefulness is not the only measure of value. A garden may feed only a handful of people, but it can answer another kind of hunger. In a time dominated by alarming news, abstraction, and helplessness, physical work in the soil restores attention to immediate life. The gardener learns the weight of compost, the smell of rain, the patience required by germination, and the exact moment when a fruit is ready to be picked. Such knowledge is modest, yet it resists despair by reconnecting thought with season, labor, and place.

To cultivate a small patch of earth is therefore neither a solution to planetary crisis nor an empty gesture. It is a limited practice carried out within a damaged world. Its value lies partly in what it produces, but also in the relationship it creates: a disciplined intimacy with lives beyond the human. The garden reminds us that the world is not merely a resource, a battlefield, or a problem awaiting management. It is a community of beings whose existence exceeds our needs and designs.

In that sense, gardening can nourish a spiritual need without pretending to save the planet. It offers no innocence and guarantees no escape. Instead, it grounds the gardener in dependence, responsibility, and wonder. Amid climate disruption, violence, and hunger, the small plot remains small. But within it, life continues in forms that cannot be reduced to human ambition. By tending those forms without claiming mastery over them, the gardener encounters a larger, nonhuman freedom—and may return to the work of the world with greater humility and resolve.
outputs.L5: Will had spent most of his life in Massachusetts, where cold winters and historic towns shaped his quiet, thoughtful nature. When a new job took him to Georgia, he discovered a different rhythm—warmer weather, Southern hospitality, and streets shaded by live oaks. Although he sometimes missed New England, Will soon realized that both places offered something special: Massachusetts held his memories, while Georgia promised a new beginning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a five-part experimental prose poem about gardening in the age of climate change, weaving together Massachusetts, Georgia, maple syrup, war, famine, gleaning, spiritual hunger, and the tension between private cultivation and global action.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. HARDINESS ZONE**

In Massachusetts, the maples wake too early, mistaking February’s fever for permission. Sap rises like a rumor of mercy, and we carry the metal pails out anyway. Boil forty gallons down to one: sweetness as disappearance, breakfast distilled from a wounded season. I turn the soil behind the house—private loam, fenced rain, obedient rows—while somewhere the climate rearranges its borders without referendum. The seed packet says *after danger of frost*. The century asks: which danger, whose frost?


**II. SOUTHBOUND**

Georgia peaches bloom under a false spring, pink flags raised before the last cold cavalry. By April, the orchard is a parliament of empty branches. I plant collards, basil, three varieties of tomato, as if diversity in a raised bed could negotiate with the jet stream. The radio counts drought, wildfire, war. Each headline enters the garden disguised as weather. Each root drinks from the same dark cup. At dusk, I touch the leaves for aphids and feel ashamed of tenderness so local it has an address.


**III. THE GLEANERS**

After harvest, we enter the field for what commerce has overlooked: bent carrots, split squash, potatoes small as knuckles. Gleaning is an old verb with famine inside it. Ruth followed the reapers; now volunteers follow combines, gathering bruised abundance into waxed boxes while ports close, grain burns, armies salt the road. In one country, wheat becomes leverage. In another, a mother boils leaves. Here, we wash mud from turnips beneath a sign that says **COMMUNITY GARDEN—MEMBERS ONLY**. The hose keeps asking its silver question.


**IV. HUNGER, WITH TRELLIS**

There is the hunger of the body, blunt instrument, empty bowl. There is spiritual hunger, which purchases heirloom seeds at midnight and calls the transaction hope. I build a trellis for beans to climb—two poles, twine, a small architecture of faith. Is this prayer or retreat? Beyond the fence: floodwater, checkpoints, children measuring flour. Within: a cucumber curls around its support with green intelligence. I want to believe attention scales upward. I want compost to be politics. I want my careful handful of soil to stop a tank, feed a city, cool the Atlantic. The bean offers no doctrine. It climbs.


**V. COMMON GROUND**

So let the garden remain insufficient. Let it be neither alibi nor empire: not *I grew lettuce, therefore I am innocent*; not *the world is burning, therefore nothing tender matters*. In Massachusetts, maple sap thins under altered winters. In Georgia, farmers watch the sky betray the calendar. Between them run roads, pipelines, weather systems, histories of stolen land and stolen labor. We cultivate privately, but rain has no property line. We act globally, but every action enters somewhere through a gate.

Tonight we leave a row unharvested for strangers. We vote, organize, ration water, resist the machinery that manufactures famine; we send seed, money, pressure, witness. Then we kneel again—not to worship the garden, but to join it. Hands in the common dirt, we glean what the future has not yet taken. The maples darken. The beans keep climbing. Above the beds, smoke crosses borders. Below them, roots exchange news.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, fragmented meditation in numbered sections on whether growing cucumbers and zucchinis can matter amid ecological collapse and human suffering. Use ampersands, compressed syntax, and a self-questioning first-person voice.
counterfactuals.output:
1.

I press cucumber seed into April’s cold mouth—  
small pale question, hardly a thing.

What can this matter  
while forests go flameward  
& families carry their water for miles  
& the sea keeps rehearsing our names?

Still: soil closes over my finger.  
Still: I kneel.


2.

Zucchini leaf, rough green satellite,  
unfurling above compost—coffee grounds, onion skins,  
the soft collapse of what fed us.

Is hope only rot  
learning another shape?

I don’t know.  
I turn the pile.  
Steam rises like a brief ghost  
& disappears.


3.

News enters the garden:

flood, border, famine, reef gone white—  
each word heavier than the watering can.

I pour anyway.

Is this tenderness  
or hiding?

A beetle lifts its lacquered back.  
Somewhere, sirens.  
Somewhere, a child cannot sleep.

The cucumber tendril finds wire  
& holds.


4.

I mistrust the easy metaphor—  
seed equals future, harvest equals grace.

Some seeds fail.  
Mildew arrives overnight.  
Heat splits the blossoms from their stems.

& grace?  
Grace does not stop a pipeline,  
does not open a prison door,  
does not bring rain.

Yet I save the blossoms I can  
from squash-vine borer,  
my hands clumsy with care.


5.

By August the zucchinis become absurd—  
green clubs under leaves,  
too many, always too many.

I leave them on porches.  
I grate them into bread.  
I laugh despite the smoke-hazed sun.

Is laughter betrayal?

Or one animal’s proof  
that the world has not entirely  
closed?


6.

To grow food is not innocence.

The hose drinks from a strained river.  
The seed came sealed in plastic.  
My good soil has histories—  
labor, theft, weather, worms.

I stand inside complicity  
holding a cucumber cool as rain.

What would purity feed?

No one.


7.

So perhaps matter is too large a word.

Perhaps this matters only  
to the bee inside the yellow flower,  
to my neighbor with three dollars left,  
to the microbes busy beneath my doubt.

Perhaps only is the lie.

A meal is not the revolution  
& still the revolution must include meals—  
salt, vinegar, dill,  
hands passing a bowl.


8.

At dusk I tie the vines higher.

Above me, carbon.  
Beyond me, grief without acreage.  
Within me, the wish to be absolved  
by something green.

The garden refuses.

It offers no pardon—  
only fruit, imperfect & immediate;  
only the next dry bed asking water;  
only my body, answerless, bending.

Can cucumbers matter?

I pick one.  
I wash it.  
I cut enough for two.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an ecopoetic passage that begins with a radio report about shifting agricultural climates in 2050, then moves through drone strikes, opium poppies, oil spills, drought, and war before returning to the grounding experience of working a garden plot.
counterfactuals.output:
“By 2050,” the radio says, “the wheat belt has moved north, orchards climb the old snowline, and farmers sow salt-tolerant rice where the sea has entered the fields.”

Static follows—small weather breaking in the kitchen.

Then another report: drones crossing a white noon, their shadows briefly fastening villages to the earth. Beyond the walls, opium poppies lift their bruised silk from exhausted soil, red as warning lamps, pale as sleep. A pipeline ruptures offshore; oil opens its black flower across the tide, feathering gulls, glazing reeds, teaching the waves a dark alphabet.

Inland, drought counts the ribs of cattle. Wells lower their voices. Dust occupies the schools, the cups, the lungs. War travels easily through such dryness: along roads where tanks grind seed into powder, through groves stripped for firewood, over rivers conscripted into borders. The maps keep changing. The wind keeps no allegiance.

I turn the radio off.

Outside, my plot waits within its crooked fence: four beds, a rusted spade, rainwater held in blue barrels. I kneel and press two fingers into the soil. It is cool below the crust. A worm knots and unknots the dark. I loosen the roots of a tomato plant, set it into the ground, and draw the earth close around its stem.

Here is no innocence, no refuge beyond history—only compost, ache, attention. I tie beans to their poles. I thin the carrots. I carry water one careful can at a time.

Under my nails, the planet gathers: grit, leaf-mould, the faint green scent of something choosing to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde prose poem exploring gardening as both “navel gazing” and spiritual nourishment. Include a skeptical inner voice, a friend at Yale, a reference to a film about gleaning, and the idea that cucumbers may be more art than science.
counterfactuals.output:
I kneel at the raised bed,  
which is to say: before the small green navel  
of the world.

*Self-indulgent,* says the voice behind my left ear.  
*You are rearranging dirt while empires ignite.*

I press one cucumber seed into the dark  
like a question the dark has agreed to keep.

My friend at Yale writes:  
**Gardens are just footnotes with weather.**  
Then sends a photograph of a single radish  
split open on a library desk—  
red planet, white thesis,  
its roots still revising the page.

I think of Agnès Varda’s *The Gleaners and I*:  
hands retrieving what the field, the market,  
the century has left behind.  
A potato shaped like a heart  
refuses the grammar of waste.

*Still navel gazing,* the voice insists.

Yes, but the navel was once a door.  
Yes, but looking inward may reveal  
the severed cord, the original compost,  
the hunger tying body to body.

I water the lettuce.  
The lettuce does not forgive me.  
It simply lifts its many green ears.

Cucumbers, I’m learning,  
may be more art than science:  
trellised improvisations,  
cool green jokes swollen overnight,  
one day absent, the next  
an exclamation mark wearing spines.

No formula explains their secrecy.  
No peer-reviewed moon  
can guarantee sweetness.

The skeptical voice clears its throat:  
*You call this spiritual nourishment?*

I pull a weed and smell iron.  
I lift a tomato, warm as an animal’s heart.  
I eat standing among the failures—  
blight, beetles, blossoms that opened  
their yellow mouths into nothing.

The spirit, if there is one,  
is not above this.

It is under the thumbnail,  
black with soil;  
it is the gleaned bean,  
the crooked cucumber,  
the compost steaming softly  
as it turns our beautiful refuse  
into another chance  
to kneel.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce five numbered fragments in the style of a contemporary environmental lyric essay, contrasting artisanal gardening with famine and geopolitical violence while ending on the discovery of an inhuman freedom within the ecosystem of yard, field, or mind.
counterfactuals.output:
1.  
At the garden shop, the seed packets are arranged by mood: cottage, moonlight, pollinator, heirloom. I choose a lettuce whose leaves will bronze at the edges, a beautiful damage bred for the bowl. Outside, the radio counts the hunger elsewhere—grain ships stalled beyond a mined harbor, mothers boiling leaves to soften their bitterness. I press each seed into its cell of purchased soil. The gesture is tender, absurd: twelve lettuces under a glass bell while, across the map, wheat blackens in silos and men debate which border deserves bread.

2.  
We call it artisanal because our hands are clean. I trellis the beans with hazel switches, tie them loosely in linen twine, photograph the first white blossoms. In another field, the furrows are visible from a drone. Their green coordinates blink; then the image shudders into smoke. The bean does not know the difference between a camera admiring its tendrils and a camera selecting a target. It climbs whatever has been placed before it—fence, ruin, rib of metal—turning always toward an available light.

3.  
The drought arrives as etiquette: shorter showers, gray water carried in enamel pails, a saucer set beneath each pot. I learn to pour at the roots. Elsewhere, drought is not a virtue practiced on weekends but a mouth widening through the country. Wells deepen. Cattle become architecture. A child walks farther than my whole garden is long to fill a yellow container. Meanwhile, I mulch the tomatoes with straw and praise the soil for holding moisture. Privilege may be nothing more than catastrophe reduced to a technique.

4.  
By August the yard exceeds its design. Purslane crowds the gravel; wasps enter the figs through their purple wounds. Beneath the compost lid, heat gathers from coffee grounds, melon rinds, the papery skins of onions shipped across contested seas. Everything eats and is eaten. The hawk’s shadow crosses the raised beds without respect for property lines. My careful rows loosen. Mint advances beneath the fence. Fungal threads negotiate in darkness, indifferent to treaties, flags, and the sentimental names I have given each plot.

5.  
I had thought freedom would resemble escape: the gate unlatched, the mind released from its human news. Instead I find it here, and it is not ours. It is the bindweed entering the raspberry canes, the vole tunneling under the luxury of carrots, the field digesting shell casings into rust, the brain’s own thicket of fear returning as weather, salt, sleep. Nothing is innocent; nothing asks permission. The ecosystem does not forgive us, nor does it condemn. It continues—feral, intimate, inhumanly free—making life from every border we fail to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
